extraction.name: FLORES-101
extraction.description: An evaluation benchmark for low-resource and multilingual machine translation consisting of 3001 sentences sampled from English Wikipedia and professionally translated in 101 languages.
extraction.license: public and freely available under permissive licensing
extraction.creator: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc’Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, Angela Fan
extraction.citeAs: Goyal, Naman; Gao, Cynthia; Chaudhary, Vishrav; Chen, Peng-Jen; Wenzek, Guillaume; Ju, Da; Krishnan, Sanjana; Ranzato, Marc’Aurelio; Guzmán, Francisco; Fan, Angela. The FLORES-101 Evaluation Benchmark for Low-Resource and Multilingual Machine Translation. arXiv:2106.03193v1, 2021.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Sentences were extracted from English Wikipedia-related Wikimedia sources, manually selected from sampled articles, and then translated into 101 languages by professional translators through a controlled workflow with automatic checks and human quality assurance.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Source sentences were extracted from English Wikipedia-related Wikimedia sources: Wikinews, Wikijunior, and WikiVoyage.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: During sentence selection, annotators avoided very short or malformed sentences and balanced paragraph location across beginning, middle, and end of articles. Translations also underwent automatic verification checks and re-translation when checks failed.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Professional translators translated the sentences, different translators within the LSP edited them, and an independent evaluation LSP performed quality assessment using error categories and severity levels; sentences could be re-translated until quality thresholds were met. The English source sentences were also manually labeled with sub-topics.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Translation quality was assessed with a Translation Quality Score on a 0 to 100 scale based on identified error types and severity levels, with an acceptance threshold of 90%.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: The sentence selection process was performed by 10 annotators in the lab: 6 male and 4 female, with roles including researchers and program/project managers, from East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America, and North America.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is intended to foster progress in machine translation for low-resource languages, which the authors note would benefit speakers of those languages.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper discusses possible bias from document structure, translationese effects from using English as the sole source language, and bias from copied outputs of commercial translation engines.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: All source sentences come from English, so non-English source sentences are produced by human translators and may exhibit translationese; additionally, some languages considered for inclusion could not meet the quality threshold.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation benchmark for many-to-many multilingual machine translation, including dev, devtest, and test splits; also supports document-level translation, multimodal translation, classification, language identification, and multilingual domain adaptation.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: To achieve the above goals, the overall construction process consisted of three phases, as outlined in Fig 1. First, we extracted sentences to translate from English Wikipedia. Second, we designed and ran pilot experiments to determine the translation process, and finally we launched the actual translation workflow for over 100 languages.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: First, we extracted sentences to translate from English Wikipedia. ... The sentence selection process consisted of selecting an article at random from each source, and then manually selecting a few (typically between 3 and 5) contiguous sentences from each article

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: Original Source. All source sentences were extracted from multiple Wikimedia sources... In particular, we collected a third of the sentences from Wikinews, which is a collection of international news articles, a third from Wikijunior... and a third from WikiVoyage

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: The sentence selection process consisted of selecting an article at random from each source, and then manually selecting a few (typically between 3 and 5) contiguous sentences from each article, avoiding segments with very short or malformed sentences. To avoid bias coming from the document structure, we carefully selected one paragraph per document, from either the beginning, middle or end of the article.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: For each language, all source sentences are sent to a certain translation LSPs. Once sentences are translated, the data is sent to different translators within the LSP for editing and then moves on to automated quality control steps. ... Afterwards, translations are sent to an evaluation LSP that performs quality assessment, providing a translation quality score and constructive linguistic feedback both on the sentence and language levels.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: We assess translation quality through a Translation Quality Score, calculated per language on a 0 to 100 scale. The translation quality score is determined based on the number of identified errors by the evaluation LSPs. ... Based on our pilot experiments, we set the acceptable translation quality score to 90%.

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: The selection process was performed by 10 different annotators in our lab, 6 male and 4 female; with different roles in research: researchers (scientists and engineers) and program/project managers; originally coming from different regions of the world: East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America and North America.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: Yet, the majority of the world’s population speak low-resource languages and would benefit from improvements in translation quality on their native languages.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: To avoid bias coming from the document structure, we carefully selected one paragraph per document, from either the beginning, middle or end of the article. ... While translationese (or overly literal or awkward translations) has known idiosyncrasies (Zhang and Toral, 2019), we conjecture that these effects are rather marginal ... This is important, as we want to our translations to be as unbiased as possible. Relying on verbatim or post-edited translations from online engines would be misguiding

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: By translating the same set of English sentences in more than hundred languages, we enable evaluation of multilingual MT with the only caveat that source sentences not in English are produced by human translators. While translationese (or overly literal or awkward translations) has known idiosyncrasies (Zhang and Toral, 2019) ... Note that several languages were considered beyond our set of 101, but were unable to meet the bar after rounds of re-translation.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: FLORES -101 is suitable for many-to-many evaluation, meaning that it enables seamless evaluation of 10 ;100 language pairs. ... Since several contiguous sentences are extracted from the same article and since we also provide the corresponding URL, we support evaluation of machine translation at the document level. With the additional meta-data, we also enable evaluation of multimodal machine translation. ... Beyond translation, FLORES -101 can be used to evaluate tasks such as sentence and document classification, language identification, and multilingual domain adaptation.
